Our Pressing Needs. 


—_—————-+ <Jep 


1. The balance of $8,000 required to complete the 
extinction of the Debt on the Building. The Directors | 
are pledged to pay this amount before December, 1899. 


2. Seven thousand dollars for the establishment of a 
Branch Building at Point St. Charles. The Grand Trunk ) 
Railway has promised $4,000 and a lot on condition that / 
the Association provides the above-named amount,—- the 
Building to be used in common by the Railway employees 
and the other young men in that important section of the 


city. 

3. An Endowment Fund for the increase of our 
Library. We have 4,000 volumes, and we should have at 
least 10,000. No library in the city is as largely used in 
proportion to its size. Because the wise direction of the 
reading of young men is so important a matter, we trust 


o 
that some of our friends will respond to this appeal. 


4. An Endowment Fund for the supervision and ex- 
tension of the educational work of the Association. This 
is very important, as it most directly enables young men | 


to help themselves. |

ANNUAL MEETING. 


The Forty-eighth Annual Meeting of the Association was held on 
Tuesday evening, May 16th, at eight o’clock, in the Lecture Hall. The 
President, Mr. C. T. Williams, in the chair. There was a splendid at- 
tendance of members and subscribers, the Hall being well filled. 


After devotional exercises and opening remarks by the chairman, the 
President called on Mr. D. A. Budge, the Secretary, to read his Annual 
Report. After the reading of the Annual Report, Mr. D. W. Ross, chair- 
man of the Finance Committee, presented the financial reports. 


Mr. Alec Arthur reported verbally for the Young Men’s Debt fund. 
At the conclusion of his report, in a graceful and well-worded speech, on 
behalf of the members of the association he presented Mr. Budge with a 
Silver Tea Service in honor of the completion of his twenty-fifth year of 
service as Secretary of the Association. Prolonged and hearty applause 
greeted this very happy ceremony. Mr. Budge replied briefly, expressing 
his sense of gratitude at the kindness of the members and friends who 
had made this gift. 


The reports of Committees were distributed in printed form amongst 
the members, and on motion were taken as read and ordered to be pub- 
lished for circulation amongst the members and subscribers. 


The following gentlemen were nominated as Directors for the three 
years ending May lst, 1902 :— 


ABNER KINGMAN, JOHN KENNEDY, CHAS. CUSHING, 
Ropert Munro, R. HENDERSON, R. H. BUCHANAN, 
C. C. HOoLianp. 


No other nominations being offered these gentlemen were 
unanimously elected. ; 


The benediction was pronounced by Rev. J. McKillican, after which 
refreshments were served through the kindness of the Ladies’ Committee, 
and a pleasant half-hour of social intercourse enjoyed by all present. 


Forty-Eighth Annual Report. 


Forty-eight years ago a company of 
young men met in the Lecture-Room of 
the Baptist Church on St. Helen St., and 
organized the first Young Men’s Christian 
Association on this continent. Mr. j. H. 
Winn was elected President, and he 1s still 
living in this City. Rev. F. H. Marling 
was the first Secretary. He now resides 
in New York. How well these men laid 
the foundation and the kind of structure 
which has been reared upon it, the record 
of the past forty-eight years has proven. 


That the primary object of the Associ- 
ation may ever be kept in mind by our 
members in the midst of its diversified work, we call attention to the Paris 
basis, which was adopted by the World’s Conference in Paris in 1855, and 
is now the platform of all the affiliated Associations. 


“The Young Men’s Christian Associations seek to unite those young 
men who, regarding Jesus Christ as their God and Saviour, according to 
the Holy Scriptures, desire to be His disciples in their doctrine and in their 
life, and to associate their efforts for the extension of His kingdom among 
young men.” 

Fifty-five years after the first organization, there are now 5768 branches 
throughout the world. This includes 1328 in the United States and 89 in 
the Dominion of Canada. The total membership on this contiuent is now 
238,000, and the membership ticket is interchangeable in all these 
Associations. | 

The past year’s history of the organization on this continent has been 
an eventful one. With the opening of the Spanish-American war, and the 
calling out of 100,000 men, the leaders of the movement seized the oppor- 
tunity of serving their fellows in a time of need, and 156 Association tents 
were erected in 69 State and International Camps, with two Secretaries 
attached to each camp. As a result 50 Regimental Young Men’s Christian 


8 


Associations were organized ; 800 conversions were reported, and an average 
daily attendance of 500 men to each tent. Recently a Montreal lady 
called at the office and left a sum of money to be sent to the Secretary in 
charge of the Association tent at Manilla. Her son was a Montreal boy 
in a California volunteer regiment, and had been wounded in an engage- 
ment at Manilla. He wrote his mother of the kindness he had received 
at the hands of the Association Secretary who accompanied the army. 
While the bulk of these men have returned, the Association still continues 
with the army of occupation in Porto Rico and Cuba as well as Manilla. 


The year which has just closed on May Ist, will mark a definite era in 
the history of the local work in Montreal. : 


The Building. The re-arrangement of the two upper stories has 
been completed. We now have 42 rooms used by members for lodging. 
This allows the Building to be used almost exclusively for young men and 
contributes a revenue toward theymaintenance of the property which could 
not be secured as satisfactorily in any other way. 


Sixteen months ago there was a mortgage debt of $51,500 on the Build- 
ing. This became a serious problem, and a real menace to the progress of 
the work. A Committee of young men came forward voluntarily and 
proposed to secure 100 who would either collect or contribute $100 each 
towards the extinction of the debt. Encouraged by their proposal the 
Directors decided to work for the remaining $41,000. On each Tuesday 
and Friday morning at 8.30, members of the Finance Committee and others 
have met for prayer to God that this result might be obtained, and there 
has been continual occasion for thanksgiving in recognition of God’s bless- 
ing in answer to prayer and effort. Towards the reduction of this debt 
two payments of £2000 each have been made, one in June, another in Dec. 
of 1898, and the final payment of £6,500 or $31,590 is due in Dec. 1899. 
It is confidently expected that the balance wili be paid on that-date. The 
Directors desire to acknowledge their indebtedness to the Young Men’s 
Debt Fund Committee for the effective and persevering service which they 
have rendered, and they express the hope that they may be fully sustained 
in the completion of their self-appointed task by the committee of 100 who 
have undertaken to cooperate. 


During the year extensive improvements have been made in the Physi- 
cal Department which have greatly added to its efficiency. A new floor 


9 


was placed in the Gymnasium and the vexed question of protection from 
dampness seems to have been finally settled, by means of underdraining 
and an asphalt covering underneath the floor. The old wooden zinc baths 
were replaced by complete new arrangements of tile and marble baths, 
including four additional showers. The old hot-water boiler was replaced 
by one double the size. These improvements cost $2002.97. These 
changes were greatly appreciated by the members, and it gives the Associ- 
ation a bathing equipment equal to any in the city. 


A large amount of the time and attention of the officers of the Association 
has been necessarily occupied with these extensive alterations, but we are 
glad to report that their time and effort can now be devoted to the enlarge- 
ment and strengthening of the work. 


Branches. It is a matter of gratification that the Association work is 
carried on at three points in the city: at the Central Building, Dominion 
Square ; at the Building of the College Association, Sherbrooke St., where a 
definite work for Students is conducted with a Secretary in charge ; and at 
the Building at the corner of Wellington and Richmond Sts., Point St. 
Charles, where a joint work for the Grand Trunk Railway employees and 
the young men of that section is conducted with a Secretary in charge. 
‘The Grand Trunk Railway has made an appropriation towards the expenses 
of the work and given the use of the Building now occupied by the Associ- 
ation. As soon as the mortgage indebtedness on the Dominion Square 
Building is removed two other branches could be wisely located in this city. 


The Staff. The following changes have occurred during the year. 
Mr. W. F. Chapman was only able to continue his services as Office Secre- 
tary for five months. He is again laid aside through illness. Few men 
have ever rendered more unselfish service for their fellows, and in his 
affliction he has the loving sympathy of all who knew him. Mr. E. G. 
Randal has served the Association in charge of the Educational Depart- 
ment, and Mr. F. A. Crowe in charge of the Junior Department. Mr. 
John Roy has assumed the duties of Office Secretary. In the Physical 
Department, Messrs. Geo. A. McBean and L. A. Winter rendered valuable 
assistance to the Physical Director for evening class work. 


A meeting of the Directors and members was held on March 10th 1899, 
at 8.00 a.m. to mark the fact that our Secretary, Mr. D. A. Budge, had com- 
pleted a term of 25 years’ service with the Association. In some respects 
this is unique in the history of the work, as only in the case of the late 


10. 


R. R. McBurney of New York City, has one man filled the post of Secre 
tary continuously at one point for such a period. 


Finance. This department has been carefully administered. At the 
beginning of the year a conservative estimate of the receipts and expenses 
is made, and this forms the working basis. ‘The outlay is governed by the 
amount of money which the citizens place in the hands of the committee 
for the benefit of the young men of the city. Our thanks are due to the 
Finance Committee for their energy and faithfulness, which enables us to 
close the the year with a small balance in the treasury. In this matter the 
Directors desire to express their gratification to God, and to many kind 
friends who have so cheerfully contributed the necessary funds to sustain 
the work. It may not be generally known that membership fees are only 
sufficient to defray one half the expenses, and for the other half the Asso- 
ciation is dependent upon the voluntary contribution of the friends of 
young men. 


Membership. The Directors would call attention to the excellent 
work which has been done by the Membership committee. They show 
an increase in numbers over last year, and also an increase of $367.83 in 
the amount of fees. The Directors hope that this Committee may be en- 
larged and that the 2000 mark may be reached on the Ist of May 1900. 


Bequests. During the year one bequest was received of $450.00 
from the executors of the late W. J. Withall. We are notified of another 
bequest of $2000 from the will of the late Francis Scholes. ‘This will make 
the sixth bequest which has been left to the Association since entering this 
Building on Dominion Square. The Directors would here place before 
the friends of the Association the opportunity for extending the influence, 
increasing the efficiency, and adding to the permanency of this practical 
and economical organization which is quietly working in the best interests 
of the moral and commercial life of the city. ‘‘A city’s most valuable asset 
is its young men.” We need a library of 10,000 volumes. Our library 
now numbers about 5,000 volumes. We also need an endowment for the 
Educational work. Who will supply these ? 


Social Attractions. ‘That this feature has not been neglected 
attention is called to the committee’s report. This will ever be one of the 
most.interesting and attractive methods by which the sympathy and confi- 
dence of young men who are away from their home and friends can be 


11 


secured. Young men will have social companionship, and to secure these 
they are too often led into questionable resorts. The parlors will be 
renovated during the summer, and the Directors will ask the incoming 
committee to plan for an enlarged work in this department. 


In many years the Association has secured cheerful and efficient service 
from the ladies of the various churches as occasion required, but now a 
Ladies’ Committee has been organized, with representatives from each 
denomination, who hold monthly meetings and plan to codperate in the’ 

; : e 
social and other phases of the work as their services may be required. The 
Directors are glad to welcome this practical addition to the working force 
of the Association. 


Boys’ Work. This is the recruiting department of the Association, 
and should be given increasingly earnest attention. Statistics show that 
16% of the paid officers of the Association were first identified with it as 
Junior members. At the Secretaries’ Conference last year, out of 75 men, 
one third testified to having first become interested through Boys’ Work. 
20% of the Committeemen in City and Town Associations where Junior 
work has been maintained, were formerly Junior members. ‘These facts 
speak loudly as to the importance of the Junior Department. Attention is 
called to the report of the Committee, which shows advance on some lines. 
The membership now numbers 169. 


Educational. A change in the entrance fee for classes was made 
permitting a member holding a Limited $2.00 ticket to enter on payment 
of tuition fee for each class. The past year’s experience warrants the 
committee in continuing the plan another year. Three new subjects were 
added, Electricity, Vocal Music, and Glee Club. French was taught four 
nights weekly instead of two. The total enrolment was 461 with 317 
different students. An Electricity Club and Literary Society have been 
formed out of last season’s classes, and this work will be continued during 
the summer. Mr. E. G. Randal as Educational Director rendered good 
service in the supervision of, the classes, and in developing increased social 
life among the students. 


Distinct advance has been made in the conception of the place and work 
of the Association as a religious movement within the Church of Christ. 
Its primary purpose is more clearly understood to be not that of a mission 
or a general evangelistic agency only, but a great brotherhood of Christian 
men, working primarily among men from the ages of 16 to 35, seeking to 


1.2 


win them for Christ, to protect, train, and develop in the Christian life, and 
to’send out men who are stronger, truer, and more efficient in all the 
activities of business life, the home, the church and the state because of 
the years spent in the Association. The spiritual agencies working to this 
end are the Young Men’s meeting and classes for Bible study. Through 
the personal work of the various committeemen, through the daily work 
of the office where hundreds of men are met with and counselled, this 
aim is constantly kept in view. Education, physical training, social com- 
panionship, all are ‘good and right and helpful, but without spiritual results 
the highest good would not be obtained. Statistics are not always satisfac- 
tory, as they cannot always record the personal effort made to win young 
men to Christ, and the words of counsel and advice given. Almost 
every mail brings requests from parents or others who are interested in 
young men asking our cooperation. 


The late honored Earl of Shaftesbury, in referring to these Associations, 
once said, “I have always looked upon these Associations in all parts of the 
world, as grand cities of refuge, placed where a young man coming from a 
distance and removed from parental influence may find shelter, and where 
they may learn the way of salvation and find courage and confidence to 
live the Christian life. I rejoice to know that the world over there are 
Secretaries and workers connected with this Association whose hand have 
got some grip and whose hearts are open to the needs of men.” 


The Directors believe that this is true of the Montreal Association, and 
in this spirit the work has been carried out during the past year. The 
Bible study work, as will be seen by the report, has made considerable 
progress. Six classes were held weekly from October to April, and two 
classes weekly throughout the year. But a new departure will be made 
this coming year by which a distinct department of the Association will be 
created for the promotion and development of the study of the Bible. A 
committee has now this important matter in hand, and a prospectus will 
be issued during the summer outlining the Fall and Winter work. 


Work for Young Men in Foreign Lands. The report will show 
the continued interest of our members in helping to support the work for 
young men who live in less favored lands. The funds have all gone 
toward the maintenance of the work in India. The new Building in 
Madras was opened on May Ist, a cut of which will appear in this 
annual report. ‘The Government of Madras has madea grant of $6,300.00 
towards the Building, and has also given the services of the Government 


13 


architect during its erection. The Government of Bengal has virtually 
committed itself to a grant of $13,000 towards the College department of 
the Calcutta Association, and the Nagpur Association in the Central 
provinces has secured one-third the cost of its Building from the Govern- 


ment. ‘These facts show how well Mr. David McConaughy has secured 
the confidence of the authorities in India. 


We regret to record the death of the following members and subscribers 
during the year :— 


HORMIDAS DAUPHINAIS, JAMES BAYLISs, 
M. W. Foro, ERNEST HARAM, 
JoHN WYLIE, FRANCIS SCHOLES,

May 26th, 1899. 


FINANCE COMMIT'TEE, 


Careful attention has been given to the finances of the Association. The Committee 
has worked most assiduously in the endeavor to make the subscriptions cover all the 
indebtedness for the current year, without having to call upon the generosity of the few 
friends who have so often come to the Association’s aid at the end of the year. It has 
not been possible to accomplish this by the sum of $500, but the Committee are pleased 
to say that again this sum has been contributed by the sfecéa/ subscriptions of several of 
the Directors and friends, and again, the Association year has been closed with all bills 
covered and paid, the small balance over being $9.99. The record has thus been pre- 
served of no deficit in Current Expenses having to be carried over to another year, since 
the Association has come into its present building. 


The splendid effort of the Secretary, Mr. D. A. Budge, to remove the mortgage 
indebtedness on the Building, will, we trust, be crowned with success, and allow of 
greater expansion and usefulness in our work. 


The changes to lodging rooms, made on the third and fourth floors, whilst they 
have naturally increased some of the items on the expenditure side, have nevertheless 
also materially increased the revenue, and the expenditure of capital for equipment and 
furnishing has been justified by the results, the property account having come within 


$89.45 of an even balance. 
D Wa ROSS, 


Chatrman.

MEMBERSHIP COMMITTEE. 


The Committee early in the year decided that an important feature of its work ought 
to be the increasing of our list of ‘* Sustaining” Members,—both by bringing in new 
men and by raising present limited and full memberships.) We have been able to close 
the year with 126 Sustaining Members, a gain of 56 over last year. 


In this connection, we would recommend that the present $10.00 ‘‘ Sustaining ’ 
Fee be made to include all Club Memberships, Educational and other Fees and charges, 
in and about the building. We feel that it would induce a large addition to this desir- 
able class of membership —would result in increased revenue—and would avoid possible 
inconvenience or difficulty that the necessary collecting of such charges may now cause. 


A’special effort to attract new members took the form of a ‘‘ Physical At Home ” 
given in the ‘‘Gym.” Nov. 4th last. There was a good attendance of the young men 
invited and a pleasant evening occupied with Athletics, Basket Ball, Vocal and Or- 
chestral Music and Refreshments. We, of course, used the usual Bulletins about the 
Building, Printed Dodgers sent out in the mail, and to a certain extent the Daily Press, 
to advertise the Association and its advantages. 


Let every member of the Association assume the duty of bringing in at least one new 
man during the coming year. Bring fo the Building as many as possible of the young 
men you meet in your home, business and Church. _ If this is not possible send in their 
names and addresses, and they will be followed up. Suggestions for the improvement 
or development of the work will be welcomed by the Committee.

*Limited members being allowed the privilege of entering any of the classes upon 
the payment of a small fee (which was not refunded as in former years), caused quite a 
number to take out ‘‘ Limited” instead of ‘* Full” tickets. This amount of $260 has 
been allowed from the class fees for this shrinkage.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEES. 


YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 


There have been fifty-two meetings held, with an average attendance of about 50. 

These meetings last but one hour and are always full of encouragement and helpful- 
ness to those who attend. Hardly a Saturday passes without one or more enquirers 
being dealt with, and we have been cheered by evidences of conversions in many cases. 
This meeting is a field of great opportunity for those who are seeking to win souls for 
the Master. 


The Committee are much indebted to Mr. Ball for his assistance in leading the sing- 
ing, and also Mr. Somers who has so faithfully acted as organist. 


An RD EUR: “2 
Chatrman. 


YOUNG MEN’S BIBLE CLASS. 


The attendance at the class: for the season was 3220, an average of 62 per Sunday, 
the largest attendance being on May 15th, 200, and the smallest on September 4th, 28. 


9) 


During the season the class has taken up the study of ‘‘ The Teachings of Christ, 
which has been very helpful and interesting to the members. 


_ In place of our annual class tea, we arranged with the several Bible training classes: 
to hold a union meeting of all those interested in the study of the Bible. This meeting 
was held on Thursday evening, March 2nd, and was of a very profitable nature. An 
address on Bible study was given by Mr. E. W. Booth, of Albany, and Mr. L. A. Winter 
also read a paper on ‘‘ The Bible Study Department of an Association.” It was unani- 
mously decided at this meeting that the Bible Study Department should rank first in 
importance in the work carried on by the Association. 


We desire to thank the following gentlemen who have led the class oh Mr. 
Budge’s absence— Messrs. D. W. Ross, E. G. Randal, C. K. Calhoun, Rev. Wm. Pat- 
terson of Toronto, J. F. Moore, R. R. Secretary of the International Committee ; 
and C. Nicol, Asst. Sec’y of the Providence, R.I., Association. The class also had 
the pleasure of hearing Mr. Niwa, Sec’y of the Association at Tokio, Japan, give an in- 
teresting account of his conversion from Buddhism to Christianity. 


The monthly collections have enabled the class to meet all expenses. 


The Committee are much indebted to Mr. Harry Griffiths for his valuable assistance: 
in leading the singing, and to Mr. W. T. Walmsley for having faithfully performed the 
duties of organist for the class. 

The following members have left the class to take up teaching in Sunday schools :— 
J. C. Bray, O. Oleson, L. James and F. Porteous. 

The Committee on behalf of the class desire to take this opportunity of wishing their 
leader, Mr. Budge, who is about to sail for Europe to enjoy a well earned holiday, a very 


pleasant trip. 
BSc Ri WATSON, 


Chatrman. 


BIBLE STUDY DEPARTMENT. 


Early in the fall plans were made for three special courses of Bible Study to be 
conducted by the Secretaries of the Association during the falland winter months. These 
were carried out with much encouragement and success. Mr. Budge took up a Course 
of twenty Lessons on Training in Personal and General Christian Work, with an enrolment 
of ten men and an average attendance of seven; Mr. Calhoun, an Introductory Course 
in the study of the Old Testament; enrolment eighteen, average attendance twelve. 
Mr. Randal during a portion of the winter conducted a group study on the life of Christ. 


A series of addresses on Bible Study by Rev. James M. Gray, D. D., of Boston, were 
also arranged for October 22nd to 25th. Dr.Gray addressed the Saturday night meeting, 
a Mass meeting in the American Church on Sunday afternoon, and two meetings daily in 
Association Hall on Monday and Tuesday, taking up as a general topic ‘* How to Master 
the English Bible.” 


On Thursday evening, March 2nd, a reunion of all the Bible Classes were held in the 
Lecture Hall, when a paper was read by Mr: L. A. Winter, on ‘‘ The Bible Study De- | 
partment,” and an address given by Mr. E. W. Booth, Secretary of the Albany N. Y. 
Association. A very profitable and pleasant evening was spent together. 


HOSPITAL WORK. 


The work of visitation has been continued as usual during the past year at the 


Western, General and Homeopathic Hospitals. At the former, services have been held 


each Sunday morning from 9.30 to 10.30, with the exception of a few times when it was 
impossible to hold meetings. 


At the Homeopathic, a short service was held each Sunday afternoon from 8 to 4 
o’clock, from April to October. 
The-Committee in charge have found it of pleasure and profit to them to carry on 


this work, as it is greatly appreciated by the patients and we believe have been a means 


of blessing to many. 
JOHN ROY, 
for Commtttee. 


EMPLOYMENT BUREAU. 


Applications for assistance in obtaining employment were. received from 490 men 
during the year. Situations were secured for 85 of these, while many others were 
counselled and otherwise assisted in securing employnient.

THE NEW BUILDING, MADRAS, INDIA.

SOCIAL DEPARTMENT. 


During the past year the Social Department Committee has had charge of all ar- 
rangements in connection with the entertainment of members and other social features 
of our work. : 

The Fall work was opened as usual with a Reception tendered to members and 
their friends. 

On Thanksgiving Day, November 24th, a Thanksgiving Supper was served to young 
men away from home. The entertainment thus provided was much appreciated. 

Two informal Socials were held for the members of the Educational Classes. The 
members themselves provided the programme and refreshments were served. 


The New Year Reception this year proved to be the best that we have had ; 2293 
persons entered the ‘‘Open Door” on that occasion and thoroughly appreciated the 
welcome extended to them and enjoyed the special attractions prepared within. During 
the afternoon the Orchestra, Camera Club exhibit, Exhibition of Muskoka Lake and 
Rocky Mountain scenery, the Gymnastic Exhibition and a Lecture on Venice by Mr, 
Calhoun, were all much enjoyed by the members and their friends. At. the evening 
concert an excellent programme was provided and attended by a large audience. 

The Committee takes this opportunity of thanking the Committee of Ladies who 
lent such valuable assistance in providing refreshments on that day and on every other 
occasion during the past year whenever called upon. ; 

The Educational Closing Reception was held on Tuesday evening, April 11th, 
1899, when an enjoyable evening was spent by the members of the Educational Classes 
in company with their friends. | 

The Physical Department has also given two ‘“‘At Home” evenings for their class 
members and friends. A large attendance was present on each occasion, and the 
programme provided in the Gymnasium was thoroughly enjoyed. | 

In the work of the past year, the Committee has endeavoured as far as possible to 
touch and interest in some way every young man that enters the building, and hopes 
that the effort made has not been without good results. . ies ee 

The Committee desires to express its hearty thanks to the many friends who have 
kindly assisted on the various programmes, and who in any way contributed to the suc- 
cess of our social work. 


JAMES WILSON, 


Chatrman. 


EVENING RECEPTION COMMITTEE. 

The Evening Reception Committee begs to report that its work has been carried on 
throughout fhe year as usual, having had an everage of one man on duty each evening to 
welcome and show visitors through the building. 

The Committee organized and carried on during the summer and early autumn 
months a series of weekly parlor concerts, which were very enjoyable, and helped bring 
the members closer together. It also supplied ushers for the various concerts and recep- 
tions held in the building during the past season, took charge of the decorations, etc., of 
a room at New Year’s,.and has always. endeavored. to keep, the interests of ‘the Associ- 
ation at heart. 


295 


As in the past, considerable difficulty has been experienced in obtaining workers for 
his Committee, but as the necessity for work of this kind grows more and more apparent, 
we trust more of our members will be found willing to help along the cause in this way. 


GUY TOMBS, 


Chatrman. 


STRANGERS’ TEA COMMITTEE. 


Your Committee have been endeavouring to extend the influence and usefulness of 
the Association by inviting young men, who are strangers in the city, to have tea and 
spend an hour with the Secretaries and your committee. 


During the past year 1898-99, seven teas were held, one each in the months of June, 
July, September and October, and in January, March and April, with an average attend- 
ance of twenty-eight. 


The teas were held Sunday evenings at 5.15, presided over by different members of 
the Board of Directors. After tea was partaken of each one present introduced himself 
to the company by giving his name, where he was from,.and the church he purposed 
attending in the city, etc. A half hour was then spent in singing, and the chairman 
usually addressed a few words to the young men, closing with the reading of a passage 
of scripture and prayer. 


Your Committee also had charge of the Thanksgiving Supper, which was held on the 
evening of Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 24th. Our president, Mr. Williams, presided, and 
we were also favored with the presence of Messrs. Packard, Ross, and Henderson of the 
Board of Directors. 


The object in getting up the Supper was to have a ‘‘ Home Gathering” for the 
young men who were away from home, and all present expressed their appreciation of 
our efforts. The menu on this occasion being somewhat more elaborate than at the 
Strangers’ Teas, the ladies kindly assisted, and to their efforts was due the beautiful and 
inviting table that awaited the seventy-five or eighty young men who responded to the 
invitation. After doing justice to the good things, toasts to The Queen, Our Country, 
The President of the United States, The Young Men’s Christian Association, Our Guests, 
Home, and The Ladies. were proposed and ably responded to by the young men. 


We believe that neither the Strangers’ Teas nor the Thanksgiving Supper will soon 
be forgotten by the young men who attended them. Many of them, coming as strangers 
to a strange city, were deeply impressed with the kindness of the Association, and also 
with the words of counsel and encouragement. E 

| GEO. J. COMRIE, 


Chatrman, 


EDUCATIONAL DEPARTMENT. 


During the season just closed, courses of study were conducted in twelve subjects. 
The 
Committee was encouraged by a better average attendance on the part of the students 
this year than last. 

An effort was made to establish a closer relationship between the students and the 
other departments of the Association, and two very successful social class reunions 
were held in the month of December. 
These social features were thoroughly enjoyed by the students. 

This year the Committee instituted the system of class fees for tuition instead of the 


315 different members entered these classes, with a total class enrolment of 461. 


A sleighing party was also held in February. 


deposit as formerly. The privilege of entering the classes was also extended to limited 
members of the Association, instead of being restricted to full members. These changes 
tended to lessen the revenue formerly derived from these sources, but the Committee feels 


that the changes have been justified. 


A statement of the enrolment and average attendance of the classes is presented 
herewith :— |

At the writing of this report the results of these examinations have not been received, 
but due announcement will be made later. 

Towards the close of the term, the Association Mock City Council, which has had 
a successful career, terminated its work, and the Association Literary Society was formed, 


which promises to do splendid work. 
H. B. AMES, 


Chairman. 


CAMERA CLUB. 


Several meetings of those interested in amateur photography were held in March 
and April, 1898, and about the first of May the Camera Club was organized. The Club- 
room is on the fifth floor, and during the year quite a little amateur work has been:done 
by the members. The dark rooms were altered and improved and the Club-room is used 
as a studio for indoor work. A competition was held last October in which there were 
some seven or eight competitors. The winners were Messrs. Pashley, Ball and Dawson. 
An exhibition was held on New Year’s Day in the Board-room and was a great success. 
Very interesting talks have been given by Messrs. G. A. Gregg, J. H. Ferns, A. Bennet 
and A. I. Rice, to whom the Club are much indebted for their kindness. There are at 
present twenty-three members in the Club, and the outlook for the summer months. 
is exceedingly bright. 


28 


PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


It is with a great deal of pleasure that your Committee present the report of the work 
accomplished in the Physical Department during the past year. 

Great activity has been shown in the various ciubs and departments under the care 
of your committee, and we desire to thank the Officers and Committee men who have 
been in charge of the various clubs, for their interest in the work under their charge, and 
the success which has attended their efforts. 

Although the reports of the various clubs are extremely interesting, it is impossible 
to give them at length, and your committee has simply taken from the reports a few points 
of interest, which, while not giving full information as to the working of the club, will 
give some idea as to the lines upon which they are carried out. 


TENNIS CLUB. 


Six meetings of the Committee have been held with the following attendance :— 
A. F. C. Ross,. President, 6;::O, M. Sharp, 6; F.W. Sharp, 6; W.-E. Cushing, 5; 
F. Benedict, 4; A. D. Kyle, 3. 

The membership increased from 15 in 1897, to 35 in 1898. 

A cinder court was made and proved a great attraction. 

The handicap Tournament was held with twenty entries, and was won by A. F. C. 
Ross. Two games were played with the Maisonneuve Tennis Club, resulting in one 
draw and one win. 

The club are endeavouring to secure increased accommodation for this season. 
A. F. C. Ross retained the championship of the club during the season. 

The Financial Statements show that the finances have come out even. 


BICYCLE CLUB. 


Membership thirty-six, being somewhat below that of the previous year. Club rides 
were attended by an average of one-third of the members, and the following places were 
visited during the club rides. Pointe au Tremble, Lachine, Back River, Lakeside, Bou- 
cherville, Mount Royal Park, Dixie, St. Laurent, Dorval Cartierville, St. Rose, 
Outremont. 


ans EE. ed

Arrangements were made, and on Dominion Day a special excursion was made to 
Ausable Chasm, where a delightful day was spent—fifty-nine members and _ friends 
enjoying the outing. 

A number of the members took part in the Field Day held on the 17th September. 

The following officers are elected for the coming year :—Hon. President, C. T. 


Williams ; President, J. J. Lomax, Messrs. W. L. Moran, A. E. Smaill, A. B. Dawson, 


F. Shaw, E. J. Flower, W. Dougall, A. L. Robertson and L. A. Winter. 
The Receipts and Expenditures show that there is a balance on hand of $22.50. 
HOCKEY “CLUB: 

The Hockey club was under the direction of the following officers : —President, F. L. 
Benedict, Vice-President, G. A. Gatehouse, Secretary-Treasurer, A. E. Smaill, and a 
Committee formed of representatives from the various teams. 

The Arena rink was secured for practice, two hours a week, namely, Monday, 9-10 
P. M., Thursday, 9.30 to 10.30 P. M. 

Four teams were picked by the Executive officers and a Tournament was success- 
fully carried out. A representative team played four matches with other clubs, winning 
one and losing three. As the club was limited to 18 players on the ice at one time, the 
practices were much better this year than in former years when too many players inter- 
fered with the game. 

The membership for the year was 34, of which 12 had never played before. 

The Treasurer reports a balance on hand of $18.90. 

LEADERS’: CLASS. 

The Leader’s class has had a membership for the past year of 15, and has done ex- 
cellent work in taking charge of the floor work when required, and also leading the 
different classes. Several of the members have also been in constant attendance at the 
examination room, and have materially assisted the Physical Directors and Medical 
Examiners in their duties. 

Kegular monthly meetings have been held, for discussion and study of the work under 
their charge, and have been well attended. 

The Annual Banquet was very sucessfully carried out, and has become one of the 
attractive features of the winter’s work. 

The faithful and valuable services of the leaders have been greatly appreciated, and 
the Conimittee extend to them their sincere thanks. 

BASKET BALL. 

The Committee in charge of this department reports a very successful season. More 
general interest has been maintained and each match well attended. 

Two Tournaments were held and a gentlemanly spirit was shown in all the games. 
The Senior was won by the Brits, and the Intermediate by the Varsity. Early in the 
season a team was sent to Hamilton to meet the Y. M. C. A. team there, who at that time 
were recognized as the best team in Canada. Our team managed to defeat them after a 
close contest. It is to be regretted that arrangements for a return match were not com- 
pleted. The Committee were also anxious to play New York but were unable to do so, 

A shooting competition was held, each competitor taking a shot for the basket in 
five different positions, and for which a prize was offered. It was won by Mr. Arthur 
Paterson of the Varsity; the second place was secured by Mr. John Marshall of the Brits. 

The Conimittee held five meetings with an average attendance of three. The 
Receipts and Expenditures showed a small balance on hand. 


30 
PERMANENT CAMP COMMITTEE. 

The Permanent Camp Committee reported that the Log Club house at Lake St. 
Joseph was completed in September, and has been greatly admired by all who have seen 
it. The Committee desire to thank the many members who have taken an interest in the 
building, and who have responded to the call for subscriptions for the erection thereof, 
and are pleased to state that the building is free of debt. The Committee expects to 
make arrangements during the coming season for the furnishing of the building and a num- 
ber of needed improvements. 

The Senior Camp Committee report a most successful season in point of members, 
attendance and general satisfaction. The camps were open for Senior members from the 
9th of July to the 4th of September, and several parties went out in May and September. 
The attendance was as follows :—first week 19, second 11, balance of summer 42, May 
and September 13, total 85. 

The length of time spent at camp by the various members for the whole season was | 
two, four weeks; one, three weeks ; three, two and one half weeks; one, two weeks ; 
twenty-eight, between one and two weeks ; fifteen, one week; twenty-eight, odd days. 
The camp was under the charge of the following:-- Messrs. A. Mackellar, C. B. Powter, 
A. R. Ross, and W. H. Ball.

‘The Committee in charge have been very energetic in looking after the welfare of the 
camp, and have made a number of very valuable suggestions for the incoming committee. 


The report of the Junior Camp shows that their camp was open from the 23rd of June 
to the 7th July, and that there were 20 boys at camp, and als» a party of five visitors 
spent Dominion Day with them, The camp was under the supervision of W. F, 
Chapman and C. S. Paterson, to whom much of the success of the camp is due. They 
were also fortunate in having with them for a short time, Drs. Harry Shaw and Charles 
Ogilvy, who are old members of the Junior Department.

BOWLING ALLEYS. 


Very little interest has been manifested in bowling during the year. 


FIELD DAY. 

The Field Day was held on Saturday afternoon, 17th of September. Fifty-eight 
‘different men competed in the seventeen events. The interest was keen, the events well 
contested, and the results were in every way satisfactory. The attendance of spectators 
was very fair. Nearly all the prizes were donated by the business friends of the Association. 


The Receipts were $123.05, Expenditure $146.18, leaving a deficit of $23.13.

The suite of rooms placed at the disposal of your committee for the physical exa- 
minations, have been much appreciated both by the Examiners and by the new members. 


Besides making all necessary repairs to the gymnastic apparatus, several much 
needed improvements have been made, such as placing the horizontal bar on hinges, and 
removing the iron vaulting bars which were always dangerous to the basket ball players, 


Forty new lights have been placed under the running track, and add greatly to the 
appearance of the gymnasium when in use, and have been a great source of pleasure to 
the members, especially the basket ball players. The much needed new floor in the 
gymnasium is giving every satisfaction. 


The new marble baths with improved plumbing and water supply, and tiled flooring, 
give our members the best bathing facilities to be had in the city, and have undoubtedly 
attracted many men to membership in the Association. 

The attendance is slightly in excess of that of previous years. The members have 
been more regular in attendance, and have shown a greater interest in their work, and 
we feel that a much finer feeling has pervaded the classes, and that much permanent good 
has been the result. Much credit is due to the able and faithful work of Mr. L. A. Winter 
and Mr. George McBean, who have devoted much time to the work on the Gymnasium 
floor. 

The Medical Examiners, Doctors W. F. Hamilton and D. J. Evans, have been in - 
constant attendance on the Examination evenings, and the heartiest thanks of your com- 
mittee, and of the many members of the Association who have passed through their hands, 
are due to them for their valuable services. 

Arrangements have been made for the use of the Montreal Baseball Park, for two 
evenings each week, during the coming season, and we trust our members will make use 
of this excellent opportunity to indulge in outdoor athletics. 

In concluding, your committee desire to place on record the faithful services that 
have been rendered the Association by the Physical Director, Mr. W. H. Ball, to his 
-untiring energy, wise planning and supervision, and careful carrying out of the details is 
due in a very large measure the success of the physical work of our Association. 


JOHN W. ROSS, 
Chairman Physical Dept 


32 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


In looking back over the work of the past year, we note that considerable progress 
has been made. The department was reorganized in April of last year on quite new 
lines, giving the boys the chief responsibility in the management of its affairs. All things 
considered, we believe the new move has proved a success. There are many problems 
still left to grapple with, and we hope to profit by our year’s experience. A number of 
boys have been developed and helped by the Committee and business meetings. 


The membership shows an increase. The growth has been healthy, as very little 
special effort has been put forth to increase our numbers. The effort for this year has 
been almost entirely one of assimilation.

LIBRARY.—Some 30 books have been added, and 1500 were withdrawn by 100 
readers. Books rebound, 200. The Boys’ Committee in charge of this part of our work 
has served very faithfully and rendered much valuable assistance to the Secretary. The 
Library has been thoroughly overhauled during the past month, in preparation for a 
printed catalogue. 


PuystcAL—The Physical work has been carried on very successfully. Sustained 
attendance and interest at the Gymnasium Classes was particularly noticeable. The 
average attendance was 38. A series of Basket Ball games and a Hockey Tournament 
were interesting features of the Gymnasium work. Over 40 entries were received for 
the former and 30 for the latter. 


Outings were held during the fall months on Saturdays, and were participated in by 
a good number of boys. A live Bicycle Club has been organized, and plans for picnics 
and summer outings are being made for the summer months. 

The Szmmer Camp was as usual a great success. In the absence of Mr. Calhoun, 
the leadership was assumed by Mr. Chapman. 20 boys ‘enjoyed the two weeks. The 
Treasurer reports a small cash balance on hand. 

SociAL—Three Receptions were held during the winter with an average attendance 
of 90. Talks were given by Messrs. C. T. Williams and C. K. Calhoun. 

The Camp Reunion in January was attended by 18, and a pleasant evening spent. 

A sleigh drive early in January was, on the word of all, a great success. 57 enjoyed 
this drive. 

A game competition was one of the new ventures. 25 entries were received and 
prizes given to the winners. The boys look forward to another. 

The rooms were renovated; new games were added, etc., and one boy was over- 
heard to say ‘‘the rooms never looked better.” 

Parties of boys, accompanied by the Secretary, visited the Laurie Engine Co. Works 
and the-*‘ Star”’ Printing Office. , 


RELIGIOUS.—-Our religious work has been encouraging. 


—— a) 


33 


The Boys’ meetings had an average attendance of 35, the highest attendance being 
90. Talks were given by able men. A series of three talks on the subject of ‘ Purity ” 
was given by Mr. Ball. The most encouraging feature, however, is the fact that quite 
a number of the boys are taking part regularly. 


We have had three Bible Classes, one of which was only conducted for two months. 
The Junior Class for boys under 14 years of age, under leadership of the Secretary, 
studied the ‘‘ Heroes of the Book.” The class had an enrolment of 50, and an average 
attendance of 16. The Senior Class, conducted by E. G. Randal, studied the “* Book of 
Mark.” Enrolment, 8. Average attendance of 8. A beginners’ Class was held for 
boys just starting in the christian life and had an enrolment of 8, an average attendance 
of 6. The total number of boys in our classes was 65, and the average attendance 25. 
Examinations were held at the close of the courses. 


Results show that the work has been fruitful, especially in the evidences of con- 
version in the case of several of the boys. | 

Monthly Song Services were held at the General Hospital for eight months of the 
year with an attendance of 18. Special music was rendered at Christmas and Easter. 
The services were highly appreciated. 

GENERAL NEWws.—A post card monthly was issued during seven months containing 
all news of the Department. A Junior Prospectus was prepared in October and nearly 
1000 copies sent out. The Department sent two delegates to the Boys’ Conference of 
Ontario and Quebec at Brockville in January, at which an invitation was extended to the 
Conference to meet at Montreal next year. : 

Since September the work of the Department has been under the supervision of Mr. 
FF, A. Crowe. Both the Committee and the boys are cordial in their appreciation of 
Mr. Crowe's faithful and diligent efforts to make the work of the Department effective. 


W. E. CUSHING, 


Chatrman. 


LADIES’ COMMITTEE, 


The Ladies’ Committee was organized in December to help in the social work of the 
Association, as well as to assist in refurnishing the parlors. There are now 16 mem- 
bers. It is the plan to largely increase this number, and to form, not exactly an Aux- 
iliary, but a committee of similar purpose. 


In the social work we have been able to assist on several occasions, notably the 
New Year's Reception and the Annual Committee Tea of May 16. 


Our main effort has been to raise money for the furnishing fund. For all purposes, 
$212.90 has been collected from the ladies of the city. With this amount we have been 
enabled to secure some necessary furnishings for the kitchen, to provide new curtains for 
the parlors—which will be hung as soon as the rooms are done over,—and to replace the 
upper portion of the parlor windows with colored glass. 


We have still quite a sum at our disposal, which we hope to increase and use as 


there is need. 
MABEL WILLIAMS, 


Secy-Treas. 


34 


PT, ST. CHARLES RAILWAY BRANCH. 


The prominent feature of this year’s work in the Pt. St. Charles Railway Branch has 
been the increased facilities for meeting the needs of the railway men, This has been 
made possible by an increased appropriation on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway 
System, anda monthly contribution from the Central Association. This advance step 
was taken in March of this year. Previous to this time the equipment consisted of read- 
ing, game and lecture rooms, and Secretary’s Office, open from 7 to 10 o'clock in the 
evening ; in charge of a competent local man. To these has been added three rest 
rooms, fitted with six beds for the accommodation of railway men laying over at this 
point ; a bath room equipped with two tubs and a shower bath, a lunch room in which 
is a gas stove for the use of railway men in preparing their meals, and a wash room. The 
ambulance room, which for several years has been located in the building, is now under 
the supervision of the Association, and constitutes a part of the equipment. The whole 
of the building known as the old G.T.R. Offices is now occupied by the Association. 
The work has been placed in charge of Secretary F. S. Morrison, and the building is 


accessible to railway men at all hours of the day and night. 


The average daily attendance at the rooms during the time they were open evenings 
only, was 12; during the time they were open all day, 89. The present membership is 
65, with pending applications, on which no fee money has been paid, to the number of 
64. Since the opening of the bath rooms, March 24th, 94 baths have been taken, and 
the rest rooms have been used 30 times during the same period. 19 meetings have been 
held for men only, with an average attendance of 31. 15 general meetings have been 
held, with an average attendance of 60... The Hospital Committee has made 928 visits to 
sick and injured men. Some of the results of the year’s work are the conversion of 


several men. 


W,. H. “BLACKALLER, 


Chairman.
